lead: A static VAR compensator (SVC) is a shunt power-electronics circuit that changes reactive power in milliseconds to hold a bus voltage steady. It exists because transmission lines and loads need reactive power, called vars: too little leaves voltage low and limits power transfer; too much raises voltage. SVCs sit at weak 33 kV, 132 kV and 400 kV buses, at HVDC terminals and near arc furnaces. The wider family, FACTS (flexible AC transmission systems), adds series and combined converters that raise line capacity and steer power flow.
prereq: You need: thyristor AC voltage controllers (AC-AC converters), the voltage-source inverter (DC-AC inverters) and the reactive power drawn by controlled rectifiers. HVDC transmission shows where that var demand appears.

sections.h3: Why reactive power sets voltage and transfer

blocks.text: Reactive power Q, measured in var, kvar or MVar, is the power that swings between a magnetic field or an electric field and the source. It does no useful work, but it sets voltage. An inductive load draws lagging current and absorbs Q, so the line drops more voltage. A capacitor draws leading current and supplies Q, which raises voltage.

P is active power in watts (W); V<sub>S</sub> and V<sub>R</sub> are sending-end and receiving-end phase-to-phase voltages in volts (V); X is line series reactance in ohms (Ω); δ is the angle between the two voltages in radians.

An SVC is a controlled shunt susceptance B<sub>SVC</sub>. It injects reactive current I<sub>Q</sub> = B<sub>SVC</sub> V into the bus. B<sub>SVC</sub> is in siemens (S); positive means leading current (capacitive) and negative means lagging current (inductive). The controller measures bus voltage and changes B<sub>SVC</sub> so voltage returns to its set point. It responds in one or two cycles.
At a weak bus, this support raises V<sub>R</sub> in the formula, so the same line carries more P.

sections.h3: TCR, TSC and the SVC characteristic

blocks.text: A thyristor-controlled reactor (TCR) is a fixed reactor L in series with two anti-parallel thyristors. The firing angle α is measured from the positive-going zero crossing of the bus voltage. At α = 90° the thyristors conduct for the whole half cycle; at α = 180° they do not conduct. The fundamental susceptance is:

B<sub>L</sub>(α) is the fundamental susceptance of the TCR in siemens (S); α is the firing angle in radians, between π/2 and π; X<sub>L</sub> = ωL is the reactor reactance in ohms (Ω); ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s; L is inductance in henry (H).

With a fixed capacitor C in parallel, the SVC susceptance is B<sub>SVC</sub> = B<sub>C</sub> − B<sub>L</sub>(α), where B<sub>C</sub> = ωC. The TCR absorbs lagging vars and the capacitor supplies leading vars; the net is their difference. At α = 90° the TCR absorbs its maximum, so the SVC is at its most lagging setting. At α near 180° the TCR is off, so the capacitor makes the SVC leading.

items: TCR + fixed capacitor (TCR+FC): continuous control from leading to lagging within rating.
Thyristor-switched capacitor (TSC): capacitor connected in steps; leading vars only, no continuous control from one unit.
Thyristor-switched reactor (TSR): reactor connected in steps; lagging vars only.

blocks.text: The V-I characteristic shows the control range. Inside it, bus voltage stays nearly constant while reactive current changes. At the leading limit the SVC acts like a fixed capacitor, so its current falls when voltage falls. At the lagging limit it acts like a fixed reactor.

sections.h3: STATCOM, series devices and active filters

blocks.text: A STATCOM (static synchronous compensator) is a voltage-source converter (VSC) behind a coupling reactor. It controls the magnitude and phase of its AC output voltage. If the converter voltage is higher than the bus voltage, the current it draws from the bus leads the bus voltage, so it looks like a capacitor and supplies vars; if lower, the current lags and it absorbs vars like a reactor. The converter can hold current up to its rating while the bus voltage sags, so its V-I curve is current-limited. An SVC of the same MVar rating gives less reactive current at low voltage because it behaves as a fixed susceptance. The VSC and its current control are the same as in a grid-tied inverter.

items: TCSC (thyristor-controlled series capacitor): a thyristor-controlled reactor in parallel with a series capacitor; it changes the line's effective series reactance, raising the transfer limit and damping oscillations.
SSSC (static synchronous series compensator): a series VSC injects a voltage in quadrature with line current; it behaves like a controllable series reactance.

UPFC (unified power flow controller): shunt and series converters share a DC link. The series converter injects a voltage of any phase and so controls line active and reactive power. The shunt converter supplies, through the DC link, the active power the series converter exchanges, and it can also give or take vars at its own bus.

blocks.text: An active harmonic filter is a shunt VSC that measures the load current, extracts its harmonic components, and injects equal and opposite harmonic currents. The supply then sees a nearly sinusoidal current. The same converter can supply vars, so it also works as a STATCOM.
At an HVDC terminal, an SVC or STATCOM supplies the converters' vars and supports commutation after a fault.

examples.question: A 33 kV, 50 Hz bus has a star-connected TCR with reactor reactance X<sub>L</sub> = 10 Ω per phase. The firing angle is α = 120°. Using B<sub>L</sub>(α) = [2(π − α) + sin 2α] / (π X<sub>L</sub>), find the fundamental TCR current per phase and the fundamental reactive power absorbed. Repeat for α = 90°.
steps: Fundamental current: I = B<sub>L</sub> V<sub>phase</sub> = 0.0391 × 19,052 = 745 A.
Fundamental reactive power: Q = √3 V<sub>LL</sub> I = 1.732 × 33 kV × 0.745 kA = 42.6 MVAr.
At 120° the TCR current is not a sine, so 42.6 MVAr is the fundamental value; at 90° the current is a full sine and the value is exact.
examples.answer: At α = 120°, B<sub>L</sub> = 0.0391 S, I = 0.745 kA and Q = 42.6 MVAr; at α = 90°, B<sub>L</sub> = 0.1 S, I = 1.905 kA and Q = 108.9 MVAr.
examples.check:
import math
XL = 10.0
VLL = 33e3
def B(alpha):
    return (2*(math.pi - alpha) + math.sin(2*alpha)) / (math.pi*XL)
a1 = math.radians(120)
a2 = math.pi/2
B1 = B(a1)
B2 = B(a2)
Vph = VLL/math.sqrt(3)
I1 = B1*Vph
I2 = B2*Vph
Q1 = math.sqrt(3)*VLL*I1
Q2 = math.sqrt(3)*VLL*I2
print(round(B1,4))
print(round(I1/1000,3))
print(round(Q1/1e6,1))
print(round(B2,4))
print(round(I2/1000,3))
print(round(Q2/1e6,1))

examples.question: The TCR of worked example 1 (X<sub>L</sub> = 10 Ω per phase, 33 kV) is paired with a fixed capacitor bank of 60 MVAr. Find the range of the SVC output and the firing angle at which the output is zero.
steps: TCR at α = 90°: Q<sub>L</sub> = 108.9 MVAr (worked example 1). Net output = 60 − 108.9 = −48.9 MVAr, that is 48.9 MVAr lagging.
TCR at α = 180°: no conduction, Q<sub>L</sub> = 0. Net output = 60 MVAr leading.
Zero output needs Q<sub>L</sub> = 60 MVAr, so B<sub>L</sub>(α) / B<sub>L</sub>(90°) = 60 / 108.9 = 0.551, that is [2(π − α) + sin 2α] / π = 0.551.
Between them, α ≈ 111.1° gives 0.551. Check: Q<sub>L</sub> = 108.9 × 0.551 = 60.0 MVAr.
examples.answer: The SVC can go from 48.9 MVAr lagging (α = 90°) to 60 MVAr leading (α = 180°), and its output is zero at α ≈ 111°.

import math
f=lambda a:(2*(math.pi-a)+math.sin(2*a))/math.pi
print(round(f(math.radians(110)),3), round(f(math.radians(112)),3), round(f(math.radians(111.14)),3))

traps: Taking the TCR output as the SVC output. The TCR only absorbs vars; the fixed capacitor supplies leading vars; the net SVC output is the difference B<sub>C</sub> − B<sub>L</sub>(α).
Putting α in degrees inside the formula. Convert to radians first. Keep the sign: sin 240° = −0.866.

Mixing SVC and STATCOM V-I behaviour. An SVC at its limit looks like a fixed susceptance, so current falls with voltage. A STATCOM holds current up to its limit, so it gives more reactive current at low voltage.
Treating UPFC as a shunt-only SVC. A UPFC has a shunt converter and a series converter, and the series converter is what controls line power flow.

quiz.q: What does SVC stand for, and what quantity does it control at the bus?
quiz.a: Static VAR Compensator; it controls bus voltage by injecting or absorbing reactive power (vars).

quiz.q: Why can a TCR plus fixed capacitor give continuous control when a TCR alone only absorbs vars?
quiz.a: The TCR absorbs a continuously adjustable lagging current. The fixed capacitor supplies a fixed leading current. The net SVC current is the difference, so the combination moves continuously between leading and lagging.

quiz.q: A TCR has X<sub>L</sub> = 20 Ω. At α = 90°, find B<sub>L</sub> and the reactive power at 11 kV phase-to-phase. Use I = B<sub>L</sub> V<sub>phase</sub> and Q = √3 V<sub>LL</sub> I.
An SVC and a STATCOM have the same MVar rating at 1 pu voltage. The bus falls to 0.8 pu. Which gives more reactive current, and why?
quiz.a: The STATCOM. Its converter current stays near rated until the current limit. The SVC at its limit is a fixed susceptance, so its current falls roughly in proportion to voltage, to about 0.8 pu.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a TSC and a TCSC?
quiz.a: A TSC is a shunt thyristor-switched capacitor used in an SVC for stepwise leading vars. A TCSC is a series thyristor-controlled capacitor that varies the line series reactance.

quiz.q: Why can an active harmonic filter replace a tuned passive filter in a plant with changing loads?
quiz.a: It measures the actual harmonic current and injects the opposite current, so it follows load changes and does not depend on a fixed tuning point. A passive filter is tuned to one frequency and can resonate if the load or network changes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Grid codes now ask wind and solar farms to give STATCOM-like voltage support. Search for STATCOM, grid-forming converter and active harmonic filter.
